title: Laptop battery pack: harvest the cells
summary: Old laptop packs usually hold 3–9 cylindrical 18650 lithium-ion cells joined by nickel strip, plus a protection board. Many "dead" packs have good cells behind a locked-out board. Open the case without stabbing a cell, break the strips without shorting anything, and sort the cells with a meter.

steps.text: Get the pack out. Older laptops: slide the latches on the underside and lift it out. Newer ones: remove the bottom cover screws and unplug the pack from the motherboard before you touch anything else.
steps.warn: Never pry under a built-in battery to free it. Bent pouch cells catch fire.

steps.text: Look at the pack. If it is swollen, hot, dented or leaking, stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium. Read the label: 10.8–11.1 V means 3 cells in series; 14.4–14.8 V means 4.
Work outdoors or on a metal tray or concrete, with sand or dirt close by. Take off rings and watches.

Find the seam in the plastic case. Start at a corner or end where the protection board sits, not in the middle where the cells are. Work a flat blade into the seam and twist to crack the glue. Move along the seam a little at a time.
steps.warn: Never push a blade, screwdriver or pry bar into the case where it could reach a cell.

steps.text: Lift the shell off. Note the layout: groups of cells in parallel, joined in series by nickel strips, with thin balance wires running to the board at one end.
Cut the main leads from the board to the cell groups one at a time, taping each cut end. Then cut the balance wires one at a time.
steps.warn: Cut one wire at a time. Cutting two at once can short a group through the cutters.

steps.text: Separate the cells: grip a nickel strip with pliers and peel it off slowly by rolling or twisting, not by levering against the next cell. Leave a small stub of strip on each cell for later soldering if you can.
steps.warn: Don't let the pliers touch both ends of a cell or two groups at once. Don't dent or bend the cell tops.

steps.text: Pouch packs (flat foil cells) from thin laptops: don't separate them. Keep the pack whole, with its board, or leave it.
Measure every cell. Above 3.0 V: good candidate. 2.0–3.0 V: charge slowly and watch for heat. Below 2.0 V, or one that heats up: reject. Then test capacity and self-discharge (see test_lithium_cell).
Store cells with their ends covered (tape, caps or a box with dividers), at about 3.6–3.8 V, somewhere cool and fireproof.
While the laptop is open, take the 19 V charger brick, the lid magnets near the palm rest and lid edge, the small blower fan and the speakers.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **18650 cells.** 3.6–3.7 V nominal, 4.2 V full. New laptop cells were about 2,000–3,200 mAh; salvaged ones often give 60–90% of that. Rebuild them into packs for lights, radios, power banks and e-bike repairs (see build_18650_pack).
- **Protection board (BMS).** Usually tied to its pack and hard to reuse, but its MOSFETs and thermistor are good spares.
- **Charger brick.** About 19 V at 2–5 A: a good supply for a buck converter or a 12 V system charger.
- **Lid magnets.** Small neodymium bars.

## Reading the pack

| Label voltage | Cells in series | Common layouts |
|---|---|---|
| 10.8–11.1 V | 3 | 3 or 6 cells (3S1P, 3S2P), 9 in some (3S3P) |
| 14.4–14.8 V | 4 | 4 or 8 cells (4S1P, 4S2P) |
| 7.2–7.4 V | 2 | 2 or 4 cells, small netbooks |

Watt-hours on the label tell you the size: a 48 Wh pack at 10.8 V holds about 4,400 mAh, likely 6 cells of about 2,200 mAh.

## Why "dead" packs often have good cells

Laptop boards lock the pack out when one parallel group drops too low, or when the pack hits a set age or cycle count. The other groups may be fine. Measure each group before you give up on a pack.

## Variations

- Some packs use prismatic or pouch cells instead of cylinders. Pouches are fragile; leave them whole.
- Some newer cylinders are 21700 size (21 mm by 70 mm) or thinner 14500 or 18500 sizes.
- Cells are often wrapped in cardboard spacers and glue. Peel glue off slowly with your fingers.

## What to leave

- Cells under 2.0 V, cells that get warm on their own, dented or rusty cells.
- Cells whose wrap is torn: rewrap them with tape or heat-shrink before storing, or reject them.
